title: fix: keep a division's operands grouped on Snowflake and Databricks
description:
Closes #439

This PR fixes the Snowflake and Databricks SQL for a division, which dropped the parentheses around a compound operand. `amount / (ratio * 2)` compiled to `"amount" / "ratio" * 2`, so the query ran without an error and returned a wrong value.

<details>
<summary>Details (agent-written)</summary>

The guarded division now builds its quotient with the same precedence rule as every other infix operator, in the [Python emitter](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/453/files#diff-63d6bf1e24b810ff8a31e25001ead8d6d81b614277ce33a5244f7a1ae25346ed) and the [R emitter](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/453/files#diff-c59fd5a08d4f58697f626df5d3fd21b80e35ce2623fa72f2088acc5ca456518d). The zero guards keep the bare operands, because a comparison binds more loosely than arithmetic.

The [shared warehouse fixture](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/453/files#diff-07997c9d4dc926971b8d7f95560004dbe21514258d781845ba7617f3f8a8805e) now pins the quotient of the corpus definition `negative quotient` for both targets. I did not add a corpus definition with a product divisor. It goes through the same code, and a new corpus entry means regenerating `definitions.json` from data-dict and updating its hand-maintained sections and the counts that tests pin.

Testing: the full Python and R suites pass. On live Snowflake, with the rest of this stack, every corpus definition returns the same values as DuckDB. Databricks is not verified, because no workspace is available yet.

Kata: whhh (the live warehouse work that found this).

</details>

### R changes

The R SQL emitter for Snowflake and Databricks now keeps the parentheses around a compound numerator or divisor ([`definition-emit-sql.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/453/files#diff-c59fd5a08d4f58697f626df5d3fd21b80e35ce2623fa72f2088acc5ca456518d)). A definition such as `amount / (ratio * 2)` or `(a + b) / c` used to compile to SQL that computed a different value, and now computes the value that data-dict defines. The DuckDB output does not change.

title: fix(py): quote every component of a table name for SQLAlchemy engines
description:
Closes #438

This PR makes the Python package quote every part of a table name that it sends to a SQLAlchemy engine. An all-lowercase name was left bare, so on Snowflake a table created as `"survey"` was looked up as `SURVEY`.

<details>
<summary>Details (agent-written)</summary>

[`EngineBackend.quote()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/443/files#diff-0f8e777d6aa8ead17a0c1afbff724be3a12b8758eb147bba2568fa748784553d) now uses `quote_identifier()` for each part. SQLAlchemy's `quote()` treats an all-lowercase name as case-insensitive and leaves it bare.

Behavior change: on Snowflake, a Python user who types `tables="orders"` for a table stored as `ORDERS` now has to type `ORDERS`. The R package already behaves this way, because `DBI::dbQuoteIdentifier()` always quotes. Mixed-case names were already quoted, so they do not change.

Testing: the full Python suite passes, with [two new tests](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/443/files#diff-a21ee35cd541302ed920aba02c6d9fc3bf674fbc6464f09cbd2ed0c00d6fae51) for a lowercase name on SQLite and on the Snowflake dialect. On live Snowflake, the describe test in #434 passes with this fix.

Kata: whhh.

</details>

title: fix: type the NULL that a date shifted by NULL compiles to
description:
Closes #441 (found during snowflake integration testing)

This PR makes a definition such as `created + NULL` compile to a typed `NULL` timestamp on Snowflake and Databricks. Snowflake refuses to add a bare `NULL` to a `DATE`.

<details>
<summary>Details (agent-written)</summary>

The type checker reads `created + NULL` as a temporal shift with a `datetime` result, but the emitters rewrote a shift only when an operand had the `interval` type. Both the [Python emitter](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/444/files#diff-63d6bf1e24b810ff8a31e25001ead8d6d81b614277ce33a5244f7a1ae25346ed) and the [R emitter](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/444/files#diff-c59fd5a08d4f58697f626df5d3fd21b80e35ce2623fa72f2088acc5ca456518d) now write `CAST(NULL AS TIMESTAMP_TZ)` on Snowflake and `CAST(NULL AS TIMESTAMP)` on Databricks. These are the types the live fixture uses for timestamp columns. The [shared warehouse fixture](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/444/files#diff-07997c9d4dc926971b8d7f95560004dbe21514258d781845ba7617f3f8a8805e) pins both.

Known gap: a sibling definition whose value is `NULL`, used as the shift, still compiles to `DATE + (NULL)` after composition. The emitter sees only a reference with the type `any`, and an `any` operand can also be an untyped column with real values, so it cannot be typed `NULL` the way a literal can. This is tracked as kata y8nf.

Testing: the full Python and R suites pass. On live Snowflake, with this whole stack, all 40 corpus definitions return the same values as DuckDB, and every Snowflake live test passes in both packages. Databricks is not verified.

Kata: whhh, y8nf.

</details>

### R changes

The R SQL emitter now compiles a date or datetime shifted by a literal `NULL` to a `NULL` cast to the dialect's timestamp type ([`definition-emit-sql.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/444/files#diff-c59fd5a08d4f58697f626df5d3fd21b80e35ce2623fa72f2088acc5ca456518d)). Snowflake used to reject the compiled SQL for such a definition, and now runs it and returns `NULL`. Every other temporal shift compiles as before.

title: fix(r): read a Snowflake semantic view's base table names as SQL identifiers
description:
Closes #446

This PR fixes how R reads the table names in a Snowflake semantic view. Snowflake gives each name as it was written in SQL, so a table created as `"orders"` came back with its quote marks, and `data_source()` could not find it. R now removes the quotes from a quoted name, and changes an unquoted name to upper case, as Snowflake does.

<details>
<summary>Details (agent-written)</summary>

[`snowflake_semantic_dependencies()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/448/files#diff-375a8ee5d75e4f2cc1d8aa63f1cb43e9469c1c01854327323a62901ff436f5bb) now unquotes a quoted name (a doubled quote stands for one) and folds an unquoted name to upper case, which is how Snowflake resolved it when the view was created. A database or schema that the YAML leaves out comes from the view's own id, which is already exact, so it is not folded.

Testing: the full R suite passes, with [new cases](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/448/files#diff-15ac545c4b4756862652dfca10cc61f86e2b1026c4ac0d160090654f00ed0d92) for a quoted name, an unquoted one, an escaped quote, and an inherited mixed-case namespace. On live Snowflake, "live Snowflake scopes models associated with physical tables" passes against the views that #431 provisions.

Kata: whhh.

</details>

### R changes

Reading a Snowflake semantic view now records its base tables under the names Snowflake resolved ([`catalog-snowflake.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/448/files#diff-375a8ee5d75e4f2cc1d8aa63f1cb43e9469c1c01854327323a62901ff436f5bb)). A view over `"orders"` used to depend on a table literally named with quotes, and `data_source(con, tables = model$dependencies)` failed with "not on the connection". It now finds `orders`. An unquoted lowercase name in the YAML now resolves to the upper-case table, where it used to be quoted as written.

title: fix(r): cast a Snowflake semantic view variable to its declared type
description:
Closes #447

This PR makes R cast a Snowflake semantic view's variables to the type the view declares. Snowflake refuses a value of another type, and Snowflake ODBC driver 4.x binds a number as text, so a parameterized metric call failed.

<details>
<summary>Details (agent-written)</summary>

A Snowflake semantic view now keeps each variable's declared type, and a new helper in [`catalog-snowflake.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/449/files#diff-375a8ee5d75e4f2cc1d8aa63f1cb43e9469c1c01854327323a62901ff436f5bb) writes `VARIABLES "MIN_TOTAL" => CAST(? AS NUMBER(10,2))`, and both the metric query and the [access probe](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/449/files#diff-ec982462992e38079ae764cf3ff443fef4eb7f22638153577151fe848670a455) use it. The type is put into SQL, so only a plain type name such as `NUMBER(10,2)` or `TIMESTAMP_TZ` is kept. Any other declaration leaves its variable with a bare placeholder, as before.

I cast to the declared type rather than to a fixed one: `CAST(? AS NUMBER)` also passes Snowflake's check, but it rounds `50.5` to `51`.

Testing: the full R suite passes, with [new cases](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/449/files#diff-15ac545c4b4756862652dfca10cc61f86e2b1026c4ac0d160090654f00ed0d92) for the cast and for a declared type that is not a plain name. On live Snowflake, every R Snowflake live test passes with this stack, including the three semantic view tests. I ran it with driver 4.0.0 on macOS only. CI on Linux may bind numbers differently, but the cast is correct for either.

Kata: whhh.

</details>

### R changes

A Snowflake semantic view variable is now bound with a cast to the type the view declares ([`catalog-snowflake.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/449/files#diff-375a8ee5d75e4f2cc1d8aa63f1cb43e9469c1c01854327323a62901ff436f5bb)). A call such as `call_metrics(..., arguments = '{"MIN_TOTAL": 50}')` against a view that declares `MIN_TOTAL NUMBER(10,2)` used to fail with a type mismatch, and now returns the metric. Typed arguments for Snowflake gain an internal `sql_type` field. A `NUMBER`, `NUMERIC`, or `DECIMAL` parameter with scale 0 (including one with no scale written) is now typed as an integer rather than a number ([`semantic-models.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/449/files#diff-4d4e6d3b4cd1dc2120e7695d6f3c5d0591e5e92aa10ef7845e34878a6008c373)), so a fractional argument such as `50.5` is rejected instead of being rounded to `51` by the cast. This applies to Databricks metric view parameters too.

title: test(py): run the warehouse code against live Snowflake and Databricks
description:
This PR adds a pytest suite that runs the Python Snowflake and Databricks code against real warehouses, and a CI workflow that runs it. Each test skips when its warehouse is not configured.

Refs #303

## Switching Databricks to `databricks-ci`

Until `databricks-ci` is ready, the Databricks job runs in `databricks-temp-free-ci`, a free workspace whose service principal signs in with a client secret. To switch back:

1. In the `databricks-ci` workspace, run the SQL from `python3 scripts/provision-live-warehouse.py databricks main.commons_ci --grant-to 61562292-ccb4-451f-8a71-c34c064f2b1c`, signed in as a user other than that service principal.
2. Grant the service principal `USE CATALOG` on `main`, and **Can use** on its SQL warehouse.
3. In the `databricks-ci` environment, set `COMMONS_TEST_DATABRICKS_DENIED_TABLE` to `main.commons_ci.denied_orders`.
4. In the matrix of [`py-live-warehouse.yaml`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/434/files#diff-3c9afb85b359b954191383e3a20e4ff96fa547fe587b59dab3befb09a30755cf) and of `R-live-warehouse.yaml` (#431), change the `databricks` environment back to `databricks-ci`.
5. Delete the `databricks-temp-free-ci` environment.

`databricks-ci` signs in with GitHub OIDC, so it needs no client secret and no `COMMONS_TEST_DATABRICKS_SCOPES`.

<details>
<summary>Agent-written notes</summary>

- The [tests](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/434/files#diff-4b2b93f37c2b4ae4677f2655c60ec60d0ceac89cfb61168c73b6d507481e908e) check the row shapes of the listing queries, how a permission refusal is classified, what the session identity queries return, and whether the SQL from the definition emitters gives the same result as DuckDB on the same rows. Before this PR, every warehouse test in `pkg-py` used a fake that replays canned rows.
- The variable names are in [`tests/shared/live-warehouse-env.json`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/434/files#diff-6be884d39f495b7eee64dff98385a98335520b23ef01a6695eb8e6794662baca), so the R suite (#431) reads the same ones. Databricks signs in through the Databricks SDK's unified auth (a token, a client secret, or GitHub OIDC). Snowflake signs in with a key pair, because Snowflake service users cannot use a password.
- [`scripts/provision-live-warehouse.py`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/434/files#diff-ee92bbd54c5c6dc85ae8183b13de455668cac6d53d95ea5ad849e052b0dca796) prints the SQL that creates the test tables from `tests/shared/live-warehouse-rows.json`. With `--grant-to`, it also gives the test principal read access and creates one table that the principal cannot read.
- The [workflow](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/434/files#diff-3c9afb85b359b954191383e3a20e4ff96fa547fe587b59dab3befb09a30755cf) runs on pull requests, pushes to `main`, and manual dispatch. Pull requests from forks skip it. A backend with no variables set skips. A backend with only some variables set fails, so it cannot pass by skipping every test.
- Testing: ruff, pyrefly and the full pytest suite pass. The live tests pass in CI on both `databricks-temp-free-ci` and `snowflake-ci`.
- `databricks-ci` waits on CloudOps CL-2949. The NaN fix that this suite needed on Databricks merged separately in #474. This PR replaces #430, which #433 reverted.
- kata: whhh (milestone M10).

</details>

title: Move `instructions` from `agent()` to `commons()`
description:
Closes #462. Also, prints the instructions out when the commons is printed.

The commons should contain the information required to do analysis on the provided data sources. When other agents use it, they see `instructions` when printing out the object, and commons agents see it directly.

No deprecation process or anything, as `agent()` hasn't shipped yet.

title: Configure a local trace exporter, without overriding one already set
description:
This PR adds `enable_trajectory_tracing(log=True)` to the Python package. It turns on GenAI content capture and, when no tracer provider is installed yet, installs one that writes trace files that R's `trajectory_read()` can read. Nothing calls it yet. The agent's `log` argument connects it in a later PR.

<details>
<summary>Design notes (agent-written)</summary>

- A tracer provider that the caller installed is never replaced. The function only reports whether commons will emit spans.
- The Python `FileSpanExporter` appends to one path and ignores `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_FILE`. So commons chooses a numbered `trace-N.jsonl` name itself and sets that variable, because R's reader uses it to find the directory. [`tests/shared/traces.json`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/254/files#diff-ac8b218a233ddf53c219c515a5d19c90469a975ff49e9d0c64c0fb3779d21366) pins which names a reader accepts.
- Trace files contain whole conversations. The default directory is private to the process (`mkdtemp`), and each file is created with mode `0600`. `COMMONS_TRACES_DIR` sets a durable location.
- Installation holds a lock, and rolls back when another thread installs a provider first. See [`_tracing.py`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/254/files#diff-b315f8a73aebb97081fbcc95955076ef3e97922f7a38cf5f9d4b08a97f09419b).
- Span names and attributes go into the shared fixture with the code that emits them.
- kata: `vxv8`, part of `bvcv`. The span fixture is `4frb`.
</details>

## R changes

No R source changes. A new test in [`test-trajectories.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/254/files#diff-785e5f42722c63ddc9607c210ff7ab191fe8279885b7b96e25d9a71d40b25957) checks the file names that `local_traces_pattern()` accepts and rejects against the shared fixture, so Python cannot write a name that R ignores. The pattern also accepts `trace.jsonl` with no number. The test pins that behavior, but commons never writes that name, so you can consider removing it from the R pattern.

title: Add a Posit Connect API client
description:
This PR adds `ConnectClient`, a Python client for the Posit Connect API. Later PRs use it to turn on content observability and to give collaborators access to traces. Nothing calls it yet.

@simonpcouch, FYI there's a tiny change to the R URL normalization, but nothing important.

<details>
<summary>Design notes (agent-written)</summary>

- The client reads `CONNECT_SERVER` and `CONNECT_API_KEY` from the environment. On Connect, the key is an ephemeral owner-scoped key, so content can act on itself without configuration from the publisher.
- A failed request raises `ConnectError`. This includes a request that never reaches Connect, in which case `status_code` is `None`. The message names only the method, path, and status, so the key cannot get into a log. A test pins this for both kinds of failure.
- Any status other than 2xx raises, redirects included. httpx does not follow redirects by default, so a 3xx response means that Connect did not do the operation.
- `ConnectClient` closes the httpx client it creates, through `close()` or a `with` block. A client passed in as `http` stays open.
- `httpx` moves from the `tracing` extra to the core dependencies, because [`_connect.py`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/252/files#diff-88e0859dcbb0f578302280d893b887effdf8649d6bf4e85e2017912fab7ddef6) imports it directly. `chatlas` already depends on httpx, so what gets installed does not change.
- Not included: the endpoints that read traces. They have no Python caller until the Python trajectory reader exists.
- kata: `4d5a`, part of `bvcv`. The trajectory reader is `88cg`.
</details>

## R changes

[`connect_client()`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/252/files#diff-a1b13721b044c31683af0d34b8fc5e21a14e8f774a0758bdba7dbb2ce34026f0) now normalizes the server URL with a single regex. It removes the trailing slashes, together with an optional `/__api__` and any slashes after it. As a result, `https://x.com//__api__` now gives `https://x.com` instead of `https://x.com/`, which is what the Python client gives. Every other server URL gives the same result as before.

[`test-connect.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/252/files#diff-8ae2dc52670f5ea7538cfc7ea03f6347b08535dc84387ceb22a67b02288adab2) used inline values to check the environment variables that commons reads and the server URL forms that it accepts. It now reads them from [`tests/shared/connect.json`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/252/files#diff-7b9773fb688edd027c2047bccef8229b79bda1bc3ca9a00cde9330249950c845), and the Python tests read the same file. The fixture adds cases that R did not check before: repeated trailing slashes, a doubled slash before `/__api__` (the case that needed the change above), a server under a path, a non-Connect `POSIT_PRODUCT`, and an empty `CONNECT_CONTENT_GUID`. A new test also checks the URLs that `connect_req()` builds.

title: fix(py): kill a self-stopped worker on macOS with Python 3.14.10
description:
This PR makes the stop watcher read a macOS worker's state from the process table, so a worker that stops itself is still killed at once on Python 3.14.10. In that release, asyncio takes the stopped child's wait report itself ([python/cpython#158287](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/158287)), so the watcher never woke and the call waited out its timeout. This is the `check (macos-latest, 3.14)` failure on [posit-dev/commons#443](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/issues/443).

<details>
<summary>Agent-written detail</summary>

- The new runner image (`20261026`) has CPython 3.14.10. I reproduced the failure on 3.14.8 by patching in 3.14.10's child-watcher change. Before this fix the test failed 1 run in 3. After it, 20 of 20 runs passed.
- macOS before Python 3.13 has no `os.waitid`. There, a stopped worker used to fail at the call timeout. With this fix it is killed at once, so the driver test now runs on those versions too. Linux keeps the `waitid` wait.
- The worker's start time is read at spawn. This stops the watcher from killing a later process that reuses the PID. On Python 3.13+ the read always comes before asyncio reaps the worker. Before 3.13, asyncio reaps on its own thread, so a worker that exits during the spawn is not covered.
- Full suite passes locally on 3.11 and 3.14.
- kata: jtjx

</details>

title: Share to connect
description:
Stacks on #404. Just getting this off of my machine—not yet reviewed or tested.

There are two potentially-shared items supported by this PR:

* The conversations themselves
* Conversation artifacts

The artifacts are a good bit easier and I'm less concerned about them. The conversation sharing is a bit gnarly right now, but should get a good bit easier as the shinychat team moves their conversation persistence work forward. Might be worth just removing the conversation sharing part of this PR and waiting a couple weeks for that work to land in shinychat.

title: test(r): configure the live warehouse tests from the shared contract, and run them in CI
description:
This PR adds a CI workflow for the R live warehouse tests, and configures them with the same environment variables as the Python suite (#434). Stacked on #434.

Refs #303

## R changes

Only the live tests change; the package code does not. [The helper](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/431/files#diff-c1bd988415d26cf98915fd557e237bdca4f232a9b529e24f66383d0f77aa5266) now reads the variables in `tests/shared/live-warehouse-env.json` instead of `commons.test.*` R options, and connects with `odbc::snowflake()` and `odbc::databricks()` instead of a DSN. A local setup that uses the old options must move to the variables in [the README](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/431/files#diff-52b44d4593af22d76d3ae512e2f7b6ca51a85ce1c0c4521d06ccbd59aa5b4071). Three Databricks tests now also work in a workspace that has only Unity Catalog, where a table the principal cannot read is missing from the listing, as on Snowflake.

@simonpcouch, in particular, if you were testing with local variables, you'll want to migrate to the setup described/linked above.

<details>
<summary>Agent-written notes</summary>

- The [workflow](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/431/files#diff-b3a24e7f275a39a6ad83638eefa1e46a7b11b90cac749002e0d280b33ace7a47) installs the Snowflake ODBC driver 3.21 and the Databricks ODBC driver 2.13.1. The Snowflake 4.x driver installs to a path that `odbc` does not search. commons recognizes a Databricks connection by its driver name, and the older Simba Spark driver reports a different name, so the workflow uses the Databricks driver.
- With GitHub OIDC, the workflow gets the token as the last step before the tests, because `odbc` exchanges it on every connection. This applies only if the `databricks-ci` service principal uses OIDC.
- The workflow has the same temporary apt mirror step as `R-CMD-check.yaml`. #477 removes it.
- The configuration check moves to [a script](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/431/files#diff-5eab78e8089571c62c978850eece2c29b04d6652f57a21e1d63fee07309536cb) that both live workflows call.
- Running Databricks on pull requests needs sign-off from Posit Security (CloudOps CL-2949). If they decline, the pull request trigger comes out.
- Testing: the R live tests pass in CI on both `databricks-temp-free-ci` and `snowflake-ci`. The skips are for fixtures that those accounts do not have. `R CMD check` passes in CI.
- kata: whhh (milestone M10).

</details>

title: Add artifacts
description:
Closes #71.

My goal here was:

1) Feels as much as possible like a "normal" artifacts pane in claude.ai or chatgpt.com as possible
2) ...but is backed by Quarto

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ebb782ee-296c-42a3-b80a-fb8e6a468b65

It also felt important to me that the artifact streamed in. (Notably, this is not how artifacts work on claude.ai anymore, surprisingly. Will have to think about why.) In addition, I wanted computations to happen eagerly—e.g. when the agent completes an inline `r ` or a code cell, it begins evaluating _then_ rather than when the whole report is done streaming in. This means that we're not actually using Quarto here, instead using a hand-rolled knitr worker. (More context on that at the top of `artifact-knit.R`.)

The agent can edit the report after, a la Canvas.

Tried to make the abstractions usable on the Python side, but does not implement in Python.

Deferring Quarto dashboards / Shiny apps, deferring "Share to Connect".

title: let describe_table describe tables outside the data source
description: Closes #469.

title: Process non-Snowflake/Databricks descriptions like those connections
description:
For Snowflake and Databricks, we do some "smart" processing to keep the system prompt size down / make the database more navigable for the model. I hadn't realized that this didn't apply to non-Snowflake/Databricks connections, yet.

* For a connection that has no `tables =`, `data_source(con)` now lists only the connection's current schema. 
* Once those names pass the 3,000-character limit, the source switches to `search_catalog()`. 
* The user can select multiple schemas via `tables = list(DBI::Id(schema = "x"), DBI::Id(schema = "y"))`, as is the case with Databricks/Snowflake.
* Make sure that relative names in data dictionary entries get paired up to their automatically-generated, schema-qualified names.

title: rename the commons-citation tag to citation
description: Closes #406. Notably, shinychat doesn't special-case `<citation>`, so it should be safe to use unless the team intends to do so later.

title: test: pin warehouse definition binding as a shared fixture
description:
This PR adds a shared fixture, [`definition-binding.json`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/437/files#diff-664f9a91705bcf48047808cf335717ad7e02e88e714a0786346df85776732aa9), that pins how both packages bind a definition to the columns of a warehouse table, and which error each package raises when it cannot. To match it, `COLUMNS(...)` in Python now refuses an authored column that the table does not have, as R does. Both packages also refuse a `COLUMNS(...)` selection that matches no column. 

This came out of the review of #283, which found that only the Python suite tested definition binding, and that the two packages had already drifted apart on how `COLUMNS(...)` handles a column the warehouse table lacks.

Stacked on #436.



## R changes

R now refuses one more input: a `COLUMNS(...)` selection that matches no authored column raises `commons_definition_empty_selection_error`, where it used to compile to empty SQL. Three other binding errors get condition classes: a metric that mixes row and aggregate grain, a table that matches no relation, and a column that the relation does not have. The `strict` field in [`definition-compile.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/437/files#diff-29b2204ccc225ac88ddcc4ab5f1608b4040a83d5c8a8c749be5d25d2bbf8f68a) is gone. It had no effect: the catalog binding always set it to `TRUE`, and the generic DBI binding has no column map for it to apply to.

<details><summary>Agent-written notes</summary>

- The Python change needs a line in the next `py-v*` release notes. Since py-v0.1.0b1, `COLUMNS(pattern)` and `COLUMNS(*)` dropped an authored column that the table does not have. A selection written out by name already refused it ([`_compile.py`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/437/files#diff-d1574f3df948b75a5c9e857ae4df96b057404b2a36c163c52718b57e4a7a58df)). Python also checks a dictionary with several faults in the same order as R now, so both packages report the same fault.
- Not covered: the "data source does not expose" error, used when there is no catalog, has no class in either package. Python users can catch the new classes only through private modules, the same as in #436.
- Testing: ruff, `pyrefly check src tests` and the full pytest suite pass. `devtools::test()` passes. Each fixture case fails against code without the behavior it pins.
- kata: 5hfw. This PR also fixes kata yhfp.

</details>

title: fix: give each catalog merge error its own class in both packages
description:
This PR adds an error class for each of the three ways a data dictionary can fail to match the warehouse catalog, in both packages. Before this PR, both runners accepted any error for the shared `catalog-merge` fixture's failing cases, so an unrelated failure could pass, and now they check the specific error the fixture names. Stacked on #431.

This was a review finding from the implementation in https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/275, deferred until later.

## R changes

The three `cli_abort()` calls in the dictionary merge in [`catalog.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/436/files#diff-ca73925f1724e7de682ebf9acaeb7b05df1ee606b803999de01da5f3cf51a02e) now set a condition class: `commons_catalog_ambiguous_table_error`, `commons_catalog_claimed_relation_error` and `commons_catalog_ambiguous_column_error`. This follows the classes in `catalog-security.R`. Each error also has the parent class `commons_catalog_merge_error`, so a caller can catch all three at once. The messages, and the inputs that cause an error, do not change; callers can now catch the errors by class.

<details>
<summary>Agent-written notes</summary>

- In Python, the new classes [subclass `CatalogMergeError`, which subclasses `ValueError`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/436/files#diff-601da732bc37acf9f3a52b9f90679c7ed48861f231221d02cc9d28f46cdcec88), so code that catches `ValueError` still catches them. Like the existing catalog access errors, they are exported from `commons._catalog` but not from `commons`.
- The fixture keeps its short slugs (`ambiguous`, `claimed`, `ambiguous_column`). Each runner maps a slug to its own class name.
- Testing: ruff, pyrefly and the full pytest suite pass. `R CMD check` passes with no errors, warnings or notes. Both runners failed before the classes were added.
- The issue also asked for an audit of the other shared fixtures for fields that no runner checks. That audit found more, filed as kata 438r (definition-export error codes) and bgn3 (gaps that only one runner checks).
- kata: 8kf5 (milestone M10).

</details>

title: Give the run_r worker its own callr folder instead of the host's tempdir
description: Closes https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/issues/463.

title: Add vignette and skill ref to reproduce analyses; add user to logged trajectories
description:
Partially addresses #428, although this is probably all we actually need from a reproducibility stance.

Assumes a setup where you have a commons object as in #414, so that PR should merge before this one. 

Instead of creating a reproducible R script independent of commons code, this PR assumes that the author reproducing an analysis has access to the commons layers already.

Adds a vignette and skill reference to guide users and their coding agents through the process of pulling in trajectories, extracting their code, and turning it into executable R scripts. 

It also assumes there will be a `commons$sql()` method (or similar) to go along with #414's `commons$measure`, etc. Ordinary SQL could just be wrapped in a DBI call, but queries could include dictionary references like `{{revenue}}`, which would need to be resolved. This isn't strictly necessary because the coding agent could just replace references itself. 

Also adds a user field to the logged trajectories.

title: Split `commons()` into two
description:
...with interoperability in mind. Closes #410. The recommended way to write:

```r
agent <- commons(client, data_sources, semantic_layer, context_layer)
```

becomes:

```r
commons <- commons(data_sources, semantic_layer, context_layer)
agent <- agent(client, commons)
```

Implemented backward-compatibly.

`commons()`'s output is "just" the data structure that holds the trusted code and output, and not the stuff that hooks into an agent harness so external agents can invoke search and call trusted code and context via methods on the output.

For external coding agents, the flow is that they'd register `mcp-console` with `commons <- commons()` in the startup script and a sentence added to the tool descriptuon. For Posit Assistant, this would be an entry in `.Rprofile` and a sentence in AGENTS.md.

title: Only render a chart when no trusted calculation answers
description: Closes #394.

title: fix: keep a division's operands grouped on Snowflake and Databricks
description:
Closes #439

This PR fixes the Snowflake and Databricks SQL for a division, which dropped the parentheses around a compound operand. `amount / (ratio * 2)` compiled to `"amount" / "ratio" * 2`, so the query ran without an error and returned a wrong value.

<details>
<summary>Details (agent-written)</summary>

The guarded division now builds its quotient with the same precedence rule as every other infix operator, in the [Python emitter](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/442/files#diff-63d6bf1e24b810ff8a31e25001ead8d6d81b614277ce33a5244f7a1ae25346ed) and the [R emitter](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/442/files#diff-c59fd5a08d4f58697f626df5d3fd21b80e35ce2623fa72f2088acc5ca456518d). The zero guards keep the bare operands, because a comparison binds more loosely than arithmetic.

The [shared warehouse fixture](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/442/files#diff-07997c9d4dc926971b8d7f95560004dbe21514258d781845ba7617f3f8a8805e) now pins the quotient of the corpus definition `negative quotient` for both targets. I did not add a corpus definition with a product divisor. It goes through the same code, and a new corpus entry means regenerating `definitions.json` from data-dict and updating its hand-maintained sections and the counts that tests pin.

Testing: the full Python and R suites pass. On live Snowflake, with the rest of this stack, every corpus definition returns the same values as DuckDB. Databricks is not verified, because no workspace is available yet.

Kata: whhh (the live warehouse work that found this).

</details>

### R changes

The R SQL emitter for Snowflake and Databricks now keeps the parentheses around a compound numerator or divisor ([`definition-emit-sql.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/442/files#diff-c59fd5a08d4f58697f626df5d3fd21b80e35ce2623fa72f2088acc5ca456518d)). A definition such as `amount / (ratio * 2)` or `(a + b) / c` used to compile to SQL that computed a different value, and now computes the value that data-dict defines. The DuckDB output does not change. NEWS has a bullet.

title: ci: install R system requirements without the Chromium PPA
description:
This PR adds a shared composite action that installs the R system requirements on Linux without Chromium. The R jobs no longer depend on the xtradeb Launchpad PPA that pak adds for Chromium. This PPA has caused at least two outages that I've noticed while working, which is kind of a drag.

<details>
<summary>Details (agent-written)</summary>

Chromium is the only one of the 26 system requirements that comes from outside Ubuntu's archive, and pak adds `ppa:xtradeb/apps` for it. The five R CMD check jobs on Ubuntu installed it too, although they set `COMMONS_SKIP_BROWSER_TESTS` and never start a browser.

[`r-sysreqs`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/445/files#diff-fc0b61546e07d4761e5975e89bd633ff917ac055076cb27edbcfb3c12dc128f3) asks pak for the requirements that `setup-r-dependencies` would install for the same `extra-packages` and `needs`, drops the `chrome` requirement, and installs the rest. Each R workflow runs it first, then runs `setup-r-dependencies` with `PKG_SYSREQS=false`. The citation browser job uses the Chrome that ships in the runner image, and its existing `Locate Chrome` step fails if `chromote` cannot find it. macOS and Windows do not change, because pak installs no system packages there.

Rejected alternatives: retrying `setup-r-dependencies` (the last outage lasted about 40 minutes), and turning system requirements off entirely (the runner image does not promise `cmake`, protobuf, `libnode`, or `unixodbc-dev`).

Testing: the action's script ran in an Ubuntu 24.04 container against Package Manager's `latest`, and `actionlint` passes on the three workflows. In this PR's checks, every Ubuntu R CMD check job and pkgdown pass without adding the PPA, and the citation browser tests (30) pass on the runner's Chrome.

`setup-r-dependencies` still prints "Missing 26 system packages" in its log. With `PKG_SYSREQS=false`, pak lists every requirement without checking what is installed, so the message is expected.

</details>

title: revert: back out the live warehouse harness from #430
description: This PR reverts #430, whose commits reached `main` through a direct push before review. The same changes are back up for review in a new PR stacked on this one.

title: test(py): run the warehouse code against live Snowflake and Databricks
description:
This PR adds a pytest suite that runs the Python Snowflake and Databricks code against real warehouses, and a CI workflow that runs it (once each warehouse is configured). Up to now, every warehouse test in `pkg-py` used a fake that replays canned rows.

Refs #303

The [tests](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/430/files#diff-4b2b93f37c2b4ae4677f2655c60ec60d0ceac89cfb61168c73b6d507481e908e) check: 
  - the real row shapes of the listing queries
  - how a real permission refusal is classified
  - what the session identity queries return
  - whether the SQL from the definition emitters computes the same result as DuckDB on the same rows

Each test skips when its warehouse is not configured, so it shouldn't block if credentials are missing.

## Review notes

- Configuration is environment variables. Their names are in [`tests/shared/live-warehouse-env.json`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/430/files#diff-6be884d39f495b7eee64dff98385a98335520b23ef01a6695eb8e6794662baca), so the R suite reads the same ones (#431). Databricks sign-in uses the Databricks SDK's unified auth (a token, a client secret, or GitHub OIDC). Snowflake uses a key pair, because Snowflake service users cannot sign in with a password.
- [`scripts/provision-live-warehouse.py`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/430/files#diff-ee92bbd54c5c6dc85ae8183b13de455668cac6d53d95ea5ad849e052b0dca796) prints the SQL that creates the test tables from `tests/shared/live-warehouse-rows.json`. With `--grant-to`, it also gives the test principal read access and creates one table that the principal cannot read, for the refusal test.
- The [workflow](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/430/files#diff-3c9afb85b359b954191383e3a20e4ff96fa547fe587b59dab3befb09a30755cf) runs on pushes to `main` and on manual dispatch, with credentials from the `databricks-ci` and `snowflake-ci` GitHub environments. Those environments do not exist yet. A backend with no variables set skips. A backend with only some set fails, so a misconfigured backend cannot pass by skipping every test.

## Testing

The Python suite, ruff, and pyrefly pass. The live tests have not yet run against a real warehouse, because the Databricks workspace and the Snowflake service user are still being set up. Snowflake rejects the CI key with "JWT token is invalid", which is the expected reply while that user does not exist.

<details>
<summary>Agent-written notes</summary>

kata: whhh (milestone M10).

Waiting on CloudOps CL-2949 (Databricks workspace and service principal) and rstudio/partnership-snowflake#4124 (the `SVC_COMMONS` Snowflake user). After those, the remaining steps are: create the two GitHub environments, run the provisioning SQL with `--grant-to`, and dispatch the workflow.

</details>

title: feat: scope worker signals to the sandbox and keep children in its process group
description:
## The issue

Implementing the python run code tool found a couple gaps in the sandbox: 
  - Model code in the execution worker could kill the application, for example with `os.kill(os.getppid(), SIGKILL)`. 
  - A child process it started could also call `setsid()` to leave the worker's process group, and then survive the kill that stops the worker on timeout, crash, or close.

## The fix

This PR stops model code in the execution worker from signalling the application, and on Linux stops the worker's child processes from leaving its process group.

<details><summary>Agent-written details</summary>

Closes kata gs5e and y06q.

Landlock (Linux 6.12+) and seatbelt limit signals to the worker and its children. Without Landlock, a new seccomp filter refuses signals to the host's pid and to other process groups, and refuses `setsid`, `setpgid`, and clones with `CLONE_PARENT`.

Without Landlock signal scoping, other processes of the same user stay reachable by pid. The application also stays reachable through its other thread ids, because `kill()` accepts any thread id and signals the whole process. The filter cannot list those ids, and a pid namespace would not help, because model code runs in the worker itself. Seatbelt has no rule for process groups, so on macOS a child can still start its own session. Under the seccomp filter, musl's `raise()` and `pthread_kill()` (which use `tkill`) fail; glibc is unaffected.

`tests/shared/sandbox-signals.json` pins this behaviour in real workers for both packages, and sends outside processes only SIGURG, so a failing case is harmless. `tests/shared/worker-lifecycle.json` now also pins that the worker's children stop when it is closed or crashes. No kernel below 6.12 was tested end to end. The userns tier (seccomp without Landlock) was checked by hand on Linux 7.0, by building `sandbox.c` and probing every rule from a child process.

</details>

## R changes

[`sandbox.c`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/426/files#diff-321eed362d19f8c27f83b02082644b3d6065d9f177c6a6cfe80daa6fd2db69b0) now sets Landlock's signal scope, adds a signal rule to the seatbelt profile, and installs a third seccomp filter after the existing one. R code in `run_r` can no longer signal the application's pid or process group. On macOS, and on Linux 6.12+ when Landlock is in use, it can signal only itself and programs it started. On Linux, child processes can no longer start a session or process group of their own, so `p$kill()` and `processx::run(timeout = )` can no longer stop a process that R code started, and `system("setsid ...")` fails. Those processes now stop when the R session ends: [`run-r.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/426/files#diff-0a0387f51156960e6088e58e4e892fa45b3d9f6c8d5ff526d29637f92cbe93a8) kills the worker's process group after every close, where callr's `close()` used to leave the worker's children running after an idle reap or a crash. [`NEWS.md`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/426/files#diff-30825fee09c3c7a36a7c4174f802736b87b4c76925063a386f868e823bf5aae4) describes this.

title: feat: handle Landlock ABI 9's RESOLVE_UNIX access right in the worker sandbox
description:
This PR adds support for Landlock ABI 9's new `RESOLVE_UNIX` access right to the worker sandbox in both packages. On Linux 7.1 (released June 2026) and later, sandboxed code can no longer connect or send to Unix domain socket files that a process outside the sandbox created, except under its write roots.

## R changes

[`sandbox.c`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/424/files#diff-321eed362d19f8c27f83b02082644b3d6065d9f177c6a6cfe80daa6fd2db69b0) now handles the new Landlock access right when the kernel reports ABI 9 or later (Linux 7.1+). Before this, `run_r` code on those kernels could connect to any Unix domain socket file on the host, such as a local database's or a system daemon's. Now connecting or sending to one fails with `EACCES` unless the socket is in the worker's working directory or the app's temporary directory. Older kernels and macOS behave as before. The [shared sandbox fixture](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/424/files#diff-9b515bf51d86fc61c6a8f3813347e465d5cbdc21994b6b2370487ea91acf4f63) pins the ABI threshold, and [`test-sandbox.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/424/files#diff-5dab783c5763123eab537941f8e123025b7e09f935b4013e51054938febaff39) checks the refusal from a real worker.

<details><summary>Agent-written details</summary>

Closes kata ctv9. ABIs 10 (UDP rights) and 11 (a no_new_privs flag) add no filesystem right, so the reviewed ceiling moves from 8 to 11. The refusal itself is untested: the only kernel available was ABI 8, so the tests in both packages that connect to a real socket file skip below ABI 9. The trade-off is that code in the worker cannot use a local database's Unix socket; TCP still works under `network="full"`.

</details>

title: Remove the sample summary from `describe_table`
description:
Closes #319.

`describe_table` no longer summarizes five sampled rows, in both the R and Python packages. The summary read like a description of the whole table, so the model could conclude a value was missing when it just wasn't in the sampled rows. `describe_table` now returns columns, types, and documentation for the table.

I ran a mini eval and this doesn't seem to affect model performance. Both versions answered everything correctly. The only time the model really used the sample was when writing string filters, and without it the model can just run an initial query or uses the values listed in a data dictionary, if there is one.

The number-formatting functions added to `pkg-py/src/commons/_rows.py` are moved from the deleted `_sample_summary.py`, not new code.

title: fix(py): read the seccomp ABI from the interpreter's binary, not uname
description:
This PR adds ELF-header ABI detection to the Python worker, so seccomp, Landlock and the user-namespace fallback pick their syscall numbers from the interpreter binary instead of `uname`. A stock 32-bit container on a 64-bit host is now sandboxed instead of refused. The 32-bit CI legs drop `setarch linux32` from the seccomp suite, and engage Landlock and seccomp together under both personalities.

<details><summary>Agent-written details</summary>

Closes kata n37s. R needs no change: `sandbox.c` picks its audit arch from compile-time macros, which always match the binary, so there is no shared behaviour to pin. Landlock and the user-namespace fallback are fixed alongside seccomp, because once seccomp succeeds in those containers, both are reachable there. Landlock now also runs on i386 and arm, whose syscall tables use the same three Landlock numbers, so a native 32-bit host gets it too. CI cannot run `protection_mode()` or the worker in a 32-bit container, because commons' dependencies publish no 32-bit wheels. The new CI step engages the same pair of restrictions the worker does instead. The 64-bit-uname-over-32-bit-binary case could not be reproduced locally (qemu on Apple Silicon reports a 32-bit uname and blocks seccomp), so the 32-bit CI legs on this PR are its first real run.

</details>

title: feat(py): add remote MCP agents and Connect examples
description:
Adds remote-only and hybrid commons agents backed by a FastMCP/FastAPI service with source-scoped grants and bounded DuckDB queries. Includes synthetic Connect examples, shared provenance fixtures, and history restoration that preserves verified provenance markers.

Validation: Ruff, explicit Pyrefly, 2,290 Python tests (51 skipped), and nine R contract assertions passed. Full R package checks stopped at missing or outdated dependencies; formatting still fails on 40 pre-existing files.

title: docs(py): document run_python and its sandbox
description:
This PR adds user-guide docs for `run_python`. The [governance page](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/421/files#diff-bfc3964ff8ee4e75bb32f4230a17ac2640e2b29553ccca447591d9583f677ef0) gets a full Python code execution section, which follows the R page's structure. [Get started](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/421/files#diff-ab18894da9379f2495d7d4883bf01eb61e175b2fc8cbd3af3850b454ba8d2b52) and [feature parity](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/421/files#diff-feafc2838b19c5a83ee9964da97ec2499f470d595ef602da6a32650870c2a205) no longer say Python code execution is coming soon.

Stacked on #422.

<details><summary>Agent-written notes</summary>

**Decisions**
- The governance section uses the R page's headings and order, so the two pages can be compared side by side. It describes what the Python worker does: the read and write roots, the 8 GiB address-space cap on Linux, `network="full"` and pip installs, the guardrails audit hook, isolated mode, and how values and measure sources reach the subprocess.
- The feature-parity plots row is removed, because #422 makes Python render the plots and styled tables that measures return, as R does.

**Testing:** `great-docs build` succeeds, and the link from Get started resolves to the governance page's `#python-code-execution` anchor in the built site.

kata: pnht (closes on merge)
</details>

title: feat(py): show plots and styled tables that measures return
description:
This PR adds rendering for plots and styled tables that a Python measure returns, as the R package does for `ggplot` and `gt`. A matplotlib figure or a plotnine plot is shown to the user and sent to the model as an image, and a great_tables table is shown as HTML while the model gets its data and a handle to compute from ([`_measure_results.py`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/422/files#diff-f2f3bb1fac5717d5faf9c9ffcb63f18739db7881dd16d9e0571093a674972bb3)).

Stacked on #418.

<details><summary>Agent-written notes</summary>

**Decisions**
- A matplotlib figure gets no result handle. R keeps the `ggplot` object, which `run_r` can use, but a figure could reach `run_python` only as text. A plotnine plot keeps its data frame as the handle instead.
- The model image keeps the figure's own size, capped at 1568 px on the long edge, as `run_python` plots do. R draws `ggplot` at a fixed 768×512.
- A plot whose PNGs total more than `run_python`'s plot byte limit becomes the "could not be displayed" result.
- The model note keeps R's wording, "This gt table is already visible", for great_tables too, so one string is shared.
- commons never imports matplotlib, plotnine, or great_tables. It recognizes their objects only when their library is already loaded.
- great-tables and plotnine join the dev dependencies for the tests.

The [shared fixture](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/422/files#diff-1f8920d95e410e8f0ca457730378008d47131978b99c4bcb0c8792492329c8b2) pins the model notes, the alt text, the failure note, and the table's data-frame handle. Its failure cases fail for real in both languages rather than through mocks.

**Testing:** ruff, pyrefly, and pytest pass (2202 passed, 48 skipped). The R runner and `test-tools.R` pass. A demo app with all four kinds of measure was checked through the agent's `call_measure` tool.

kata: zecq (closes on merge)
</details>

## R changes

R's code is unchanged. A ggplot or gt table that a measure returns now shows at full opacity, because the shared stylesheet's override for shinychat's dimming of finished tool cards names their classes as well as run_r's plots; before, both were faded. The other R change is a [new test](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/422/files#diff-fb2eac4a0e7450a6d910c43af42f6dee0e9778d365c8f36fc8115cd969a9f119) that runs the shared fixture's four cases (a `ggplot`, a `ggplot` that fails to build, a `gt` table, and a `gt` table whose formatter errors) through `call_measure_tool()`, so R's existing behaviour is now the contract Python is checked against.

title: test: pin the execution tool's output and worker failures in shared fixtures
description:
This PR adds two shared fixtures for code execution, which both packages test against a real worker. [`execution-repl.json`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/418/files#diff-d9ca85cfd93074ab18960b1c58d38a816646c92b6a0e28773c08858c58e25f11) pins what the model reads back from `run_r` and `run_python`. [`worker-lifecycle.json`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/418/files#diff-dde5f18a2df018d4beff9979d06449d63d1494c46722cf65ae8938bd4311d13e) pins the worker's time limits and the messages for a timed-out or crashed call.

Stacked on #417.

<details><summary>Agent-written notes</summary>

**Decisions**
- Three differences between the REPLs are left out of the fixture on purpose, and the fixture lists them. R shows every visible top-level value, as its console does, and Python shows only the trailing one, as IPython does. R puts two writes to the same line on separate lines. An error is R's condition message but Python's traceback, so that case compares only the first and last lines.
- Values print each language's own way (`[1] 3` and `3`), and R keeps the newline that ends printed text when it joins the next output (`"working\n\n[1] 42"` where Python gives `"working\n42"`). A case that shows either gives the text for each language, so neither package's output changes.
- The fixture leaves out failures that only one driver can detect: Python's stop button, its reply-out-of-turn check, and the restart note after a stopped call. R has no stop path, so there is nothing for it to agree with yet.
- The time limit in the messages is always a whole number of seconds in the fixture. R formats it as an integer and Python with `:g`, so the two would differ only for a fractional limit.
- Neither package reads the fixture at run time. Each keeps its own constants and strings, and its runner checks them against the fixture.

**Testing:** ruff, pyrefly, and pytest pass (2192 passed, 48 skipped). The full R testthat suite passes with `NOT_CRAN=true` (0 failures). The R suite ran against the branch installed into a scratch library, because the worker loads commons from the library. The Python runners skip on hosts that cannot sandbox a worker, as the driver tests do. The R runner skips the unresponsive case on Windows, which has no SIGSTOP.

kata: y154, 0z62 (both close on merge)
</details>

## R changes

@simonpcouch, tiny change on the R side. All behavior is the same as before. The worker's default time limits are now in one `worker_defaults` list in [run-r.R](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/418/files#diff-0a0387f51156960e6088e58e4e892fa45b3d9f6c8d5ff526d29637f92cbe93a8), with the same values, so the [new runner](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/418/files#diff-3524b199576692b12fb95747edc82eed0ac68353f0cef4dc05aa02ae68007bce) can check them against the fixture.

title: feat(py): add run_python, which runs model code in the agent's sandboxed session
description:
This PR wires up the python code execution functionality by adding the `run_python` tool, which lets a `Commons` agent run the model's Python code in a sandboxed session and shows the code, its output, and any matplotlib plots in the chat. `Commons` gains a `network` argument (`"none"` or `"full"`) that sets whether that session can reach the network. It also lets sandboxed code in both packages start child processes on macOS, which `run_python` needs to install packages.

Stacked on #415.

<details><summary>Agent-written notes</summary>

**Decisions**
- The session runs on its own event loop in a background thread, and the agent registers `run_python` as an async tool, so `stream_async()` never blocks the caller's loop. chatlas refuses a sync `chat()` while an async tool is registered, so `Commons.chat()` uses a sync version of the tool for the length of the call. As a result, Python's `chat()` can run code, and R's cannot.
- Building a `Commons` also builds the worker, so a host that cannot sandbox the session (Windows, or Linux without seccomp or without Landlock and user namespaces) fails at construction unless `COMMONS_ALLOW_UNSAFE_FALLBACK` is set. Such hosts could build an agent before this PR. R behaves the same way, but R's trusted-only mode skips the worker; Python has no such mode yet, so the opt-in is the only way through until it does.
- The tool description asks the session's interpreter whether matplotlib and pip are importable, and adjusts its plot and install rules to match. It offers the install rule only when the network is on and the session is sandboxed, because the guardrails fallback refuses child processes.
- With `network="full"`, the model installs packages by running `python -m pip install --target` in a child process. Running pip inside the session stops working in pip 26.3: an in-process install adds a permanent import hook that makes every later non-stdlib import raise. Child processes needed one sandbox rule on macOS (see the R section), and Linux already allowed them.
- `run_sql` and `call_metrics` results are stored as a pandas data frame (polars, then a pyarrow Table, when pandas is missing). They were lists of rows, so `r1` was not a frame, and a result with a date or `Decimal` column reached the session only as text.
- The chat's stop button stops a running call. The worker interrupts it, as it does on a timeout, and keeps the session and its variables if the call answers within the grace period. Otherwise it restarts the session, and the next result tells the model its variables were reset.
- On macOS the session sets `MPL_IGNORE_SYSTEM_FONTS`, because matplotlib's system font listing runs `system_profiler` and adds about 7 s to each session's first plot. Plots use matplotlib's bundled fonts there, so text those fonts lack (CJK, for example) renders as boxes.
- The display CSS classes are renamed from `commons-run-r-*` to `commons-run-*`, so both packages use the same names. shinychat renders finished tool cards at 70% opacity, so a card that holds a plot is now shown at full opacity.
- The lock moves to shinychat 0.7.2.

**Left out**
- A shared fixture for the REPL behaviour. A follow-up PR stacked on this one adds it. The child-process sandbox behaviour is pinned by each package's own tests until the shared sandbox fixture lands.
- The governance and feature-parity docs pages still say Python has no code execution. A separate docs task rewrites them.
- The shared system prompt invites charts even when matplotlib is missing. This is rare, and the tool description says plots are unavailable.
- Plot alt text is generic in both packages.

**Testing:** ruff, pyrefly, and the full pytest suite pass (2184 passed, 48 skipped), and the cancel tests also pass on Python 3.11. R's sandbox tests pass locally on macOS, and they fail without the new sandbox rule; R CMD check is left to CI. The child-process install was run in the sandbox on macOS and in a Linux container. Every prompt in a manual test app was run against a live model with the network on: handles with date columns, plots, output order, measure sources, errors, a package install, and a stop mid-call that kept the session.

kata: 2q9b (closes 52dt and 1bph on merge; follow-ups: 4r4a for trusted-only mode, dkev for the shared sandbox fixture)
</details>

## R changes

@simonpcouch 

**CSS class names.** The CSS classes used by `run_r` are renamed so they can be shared with `run_python`.
Class names are now `commons-run-display`, `commons-run-details`, `commons-run-code`, and `commons-run-plot` instead of `commons-run-r-*`. The same inputs give the same HTML apart from the class names. App CSS that existing commons apps have already written to target the old names will stop matching (mentioned in [NEWS.md](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/417/files#diff-30825fee09c3c7a36a7c4174f802736b87b4c76925063a386f868e823bf5aae4), though we can remove it if not important enough for that file). See [run-r.R](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/417/files#diff-0a0387f51156960e6088e58e4e892fa45b3d9f6c8d5ff526d29637f92cbe93a8) and the [stylesheet](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/417/files#diff-d624b64e6a4f3ae3e9325f3aa14badf94c6b6c2b6ad9894e8e227980c5f8cadb). The same stylesheet now shows a tool card that holds a plot at full opacity, so `run_r` plots are no longer faded once the call finishes.

**Child processes on macOS.** The macOS sandbox now lets the R session start other programs. Before, `system()` and `system2()` from `run_r` code failed on macOS, because a new process reads the root directory as it starts and the sandbox denied that read. I found this gap while building the Python sandbox, and changed R as well so the two implementations match. Linux already allowed child processes in both, so this appears to have been an unintended gap. The [sandbox profile](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/417/files#diff-321eed362d19f8c27f83b02082644b3d6065d9f177c6a6cfe80daa6fd2db69b0) now allows reading the root directory itself. That shows the names at the top level of the disk, but not the contents of anything under them, and child processes run under the same sandbox. In the [sandbox tests](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/417/files#diff-5dab783c5763123eab537941f8e123025b7e09f935b4013e51054938febaff39), the existing check that a child process can run now also runs on macOS, and its probe uses `/bin/sh` because macOS has no `/bin/true`. NEWS has a bullet.

title: fix(py): kill a worker that stops itself instead of freezing the host
description:
This PR stops model code from freezing the host by stopping its own worker (`os.kill(os.getpid(), signal.SIGSTOP)`). Each local worker now gets a thread that kills the worker's process group when it stops, and the call reports a crash.

Stacked on #411.

<details><summary>Agent-written details</summary>

**Why the host froze.** On macOS, Python 3.14's asyncio treats `waitid()`'s report of a stopped child as an exit. It then calls a blocking `waitpid()` on the event-loop thread, which waits until the child really exits. Killing the stopped worker ends that wait. The reasoning is in the docstring of `_kill_when_stopped` ([diff](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/415/files#diff-b7495093e0e057b37fe0631692e47da10a2292afe93b4c9acbc645d29f02ba93)).

**Same behaviour on every platform.** The guard runs wherever `os.waitid` exists (Linux, and macOS from 3.13). A stopped worker is therefore reported as a crash on every platform, rather than as a call timeout on Linux. macOS on 3.11 and 3.12 has no `os.waitid`, so there a stopped worker still runs into the call timeout. asyncio on those versions does not freeze.

**Rejected alternatives:**
- Denying self-signals in the seatbelt profile. A child of the worker can still stop it, and the unsafe opt-in has no sandbox.
- Replacing asyncio's child watcher with a kqueue exit watch. That would add a second way to spawn the worker.

**Tests.** The write-bound test used SIGSTOP to make the worker stop reading. It now uses a stand-in worker that announces it's ready and never reads stdin. The new self-stop test hangs on 3.14 without the fix and passes with it. ruff, pyrefly, and the full suite pass, and the driver tests also pass on 3.14.

kata: d5sr
</details>

title: feat(py): capture matplotlib plots in the worker's ordered output
description:
This PR adds plot capture to the Python execution worker. Figures a call draws come back as PNG images, in order with the text the call printed. This is the worker and protocol half of plotting; the `run_python` tool that shows plots to the model and the user comes separately.

**Review notes**

- `Result` and `Error` replace `stdout`/`stderr` with `output`, an ordered tuple of text and plot segments ([`_protocol.py`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/411/files#diff-a0519f8ef9c93c31dc9b8f4a8b068ebffa1c755185a6bbc927da0c29fd9b4431), captured by [`_repl.py`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/411/files#diff-42f28f470546bf1d8b33de0eab998dd16123dd51159484c9f93b39b73c05518f)). This is internal API, and every caller is updated.
- A figure enters the output at `plt.show()` or when the call ends, which is how Jupyter behaves ([`_plots.py`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/411/files#diff-b63d40d6c45b930889aab5d4f41289ef1974ba7206abd2988a6f768e00e79161)). R also flushes a plot when text follows it; matplotlib edits figures in place, so doing that here would capture half-built figures.
- Plots keep the figure's own size (matplotlib's default is 640×480), with the model image's long edge capped at 1568 px and a 2× image for display. R uses a fixed 768×512 device. This difference is deliberate, and it will be recorded when `run_python` lands.
- A call returns at most 20 plots and 16 MiB of PNG data. The driver checks both again, along with each image's PNG header.

**Testing**

The full Python suite passes on macOS under seatbelt. The execution tests pass on Linux under Landlock and seccomp, run in a container, and guardrails mode is covered too. matplotlib is a dev dependency only.

Some manual testing: 
 - [demo_plot_capture.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33271754/demo_plot_capture.py)
 - [plot-capture-demo.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33271744/plot-capture-demo.html)


<details><summary>Agent-written detail</summary>

kata: fj8r (this work); ky4s (an `Error` now includes what the call printed before it raised, so this closes it too); 2q9b (`run_python`, which will consume `output`).

Each figure is rendered twice (the model PNG and a 2× display PNG), then closed. Failures from model code (a broken artist, a replaced `savefig` or `plt.close`, a broken pyplot, an exception whose `repr` fails) cost only the affected figure and add a stderr note where the figure would have been. They never end the session.

</details>

title: refactor(py): remove interpreter_warning(), which nothing calls

**Testing:** ruff, pyrefly, and pytest pass (2033 passed, 50 skipped).

kata: 2wnv (closes on merge)
</details>

title: feat(py): add Worker, which runs model code in a persistent sandboxed Python session
description:
This PR adds [`Worker`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/387/files#diff-f781b854901826ded46315fd8826a9a242344847dc516ca56881b107bf8fb7ac), which runs one persistent Python session in a sandboxed child process. The process starts on the first call and closes after 10 idle minutes. When a call times out, the worker interrupts it, and restarts the process only if the interrupt gets no answer.

`Worker` does not start the Python process itself. It asks a [backend](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/387/files#diff-b7495093e0e057b37fe0631692e47da10a2292afe93b4c9acbc645d29f02ba93) for one. The only backend today, `LocalBackend`, runs the process on this machine: it sets up the process's scratch folder, environment, and sandbox, and stops the process when asked. A backend that runs the process in a container could replace it later, with no change to `Worker`. This PR also removes the backend's `exec()` method, which was an errant addition in a previous PR that had no callers yet.

On a host that cannot sandbox, a user who opts in with `COMMONS_ALLOW_UNSAFE_FALLBACK` now gets [guardrails](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/387/files#diff-a2c37a4646c57c8c7c90654d72f15878f88a394119576fd4bdc40ad3ff1be087): best-effort checks on files, processes, and the network. They are not a security boundary.

It also corrects a fault on `main` that stopped the worker from starting on stock Ubuntu. The [Landlock sandbox](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/387/files#diff-46909da064f862a27cb10ecbec4ba90968e64d21a1c5be5925d375bf4fd09651) asked for directory rights on a file, and the kernel refused the rule.

<details>
<summary>Details (agent-written)</summary>

- Calls run one at a time. A pending count stops the idle reap from closing a worker while a call waits or runs.
- The two timeout outcomes give the model different messages. An interrupted session keeps its variables, and a restarted session loses them. The [worker](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/387/files#diff-1a05819857e509d3d6963db260af9c33b059c7b85c8bd7ff36476044c2f73124) raises `KeyboardInterrupt` only while model code runs, so an interrupt that comes as a call ends cannot lose the reply or the session. Every other failure message names its cause: code too large to send (the session stays), a worker that stopped answering, or a start that failed, with the worker's stderr.
- The worker defines the measure sources again at every start, so a restarted worker has the same definitions as the first one. The [harvested source](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/387/files#diff-4d3d50db42eb5232fcc93a7ff8258dca9b72f925f9678fd356c1311ad219fe7b) has no decorators or indent, and source that does not parse is kept as a comment. A default of a def or lambda that raises is replaced by a placeholder, which raises `NameError` only when the measure uses it. A source that still fails to define is skipped. The model reads a measure's source with `inspect.getsource(name)`, because the worker registers each source's text with `linecache`.
- Each handle that the worker does not have goes in its own message before the call, so each message stays under the channel limit. A handle too large for the channel, or one the worker cannot decode, is skipped.
- When the worker exits, `LocalSession` kills the rest of its process group at once, so a child left by a crash, or one that ignores SIGTERM, does not outlive it.
- Guardrails are an audit hook, active only while model code runs. They deny reads outside the sandbox's read roots, writes outside the scratch directory, process creation, and network access under `network="none"`, and raise `PermissionError`. The read roots are the Python sandbox's, which are wider than those of R's `worker_guardrails()`.
- The R package implements the same lifecycle in `run_r_tool()` and `worker_await()` in `pkg-r/R/run-r.R`. A shared fixture for the timeouts and messages both drivers use is tracked as kata y154, for the wiring PR.
- Landlock: the sandbox follows each symlink in a read root one level down, so `/bin/pkill` resolves to the regular file `/usr/bin/pgrep`. The kernel accepts only file rights in a rule on a file. `add_roots` in `pkg-r/src/sandbox.c` does not limit a file's rights either. This PR does not change it.
- Known gap: on macOS with Python 3.14, a stopped worker blocks the host's event loop, because asyncio reads the `waitid()` report of a stopped child as an exit. The SIGSTOP test is skipped there. Tracked as kata d5sr.
- Other residuals are tracked outside this PR: a child that calls `setsid()` escapes the process-group kill (kata y06q), the worker can signal its parent (kata gs5e), and model code can reach the protocol descriptors (recorded on kata bgk1).
- Left out of this PR: the read roots include the directories of editable installs, and the macOS `/dev` root (shared with R) lets model code open other terminals. A worker that exits between calls restarts with no message to the model, as in R.
- CI jobs have a time limit, and a test that stalls for 5 minutes prints every thread's stack.
- kata: bgk1
- Verification: ruff, pyrefly, and pytest pass on macOS, and the execution suites pass in a Linux container.

</details>


## Lifecycle state diagram

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "No process" as none
    none : Worker._session is None

    state "Starting" as starting
    starting : Worker._ensure()
    starting : LocalBackend.start() spawns _runtime/_worker.py
    starting : waits for Ready, then Worker._define() per measure source

    state "Running a call" as running
    running : Worker._call()
    running : Worker._sync() sends each new handle in its own Call
    running : Worker._send(Call), then Worker._await_reply()

    state "Idle" as idle
    idle : Worker._schedule_reap() timer is running

    state "Interrupting" as interrupting
    interrupting : Worker._escalate()
    interrupting : LocalSession.interrupt() sends SIGINT to the process group

    state "Shutting down" as closing
    closing : Worker._shutdown() then LocalSession.close()
    closing : _terminate() sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL
    closing : LocalSession._kill_group() kills any children left
    closing : scratch directory removed

    [*] --> none
    none --> starting: Worker.run()
    starting --> running: Ready, sources defined
    starting --> closing: SPAWN_TIMEOUT 30 s, raises RuntimeError
    idle --> running: Worker.run()
    running --> idle: Result or Error
    running --> interrupting: CALL_TIMEOUT 60 s
    interrupting --> idle: reply within INTERRUPT_GRACE 5 s, variables kept
    interrupting --> closing: no reply, Failure, variables lost
    running --> closing: crash or bad reply, Failure
    idle --> closing: IDLE_TIMEOUT 10 min, Worker._reap_when_idle()
    closing --> none
```

title: fix: screen CLONE_NEWTIME in the worker's seccomp filters
description:
This PR adds `CLONE_NEWTIME` (0x80) to the namespace-flag mask of both worker seccomp filters, closing a gap found during the Python implementation where clone() with that bit set passed a filter that intends to refuse namespace creation.

> (FYI, because I was not aware...) `CLONE_NEWTIME` is the clone() flag that asks for a new time namespace, which gives a process its own view of the monotonic and boot-time clocks. The filter blocks namespace flags because a worker that can create namespaces can step out of the filesystem sandbox expressed in them. 

<details>
<summary>Agent-written detail: design notes and verification</summary>

kata `3rga`.

**Review notes**

- The legacy clone ABI cannot actually create a time namespace: the kernel strips the CSIGNAL byte (the 0x80 bit included) from the flags before the namespace logic runs, so the live creation paths are unshare (screened outright) and clone3 (denied ENOSYS). The mask change completes the screen's stated intent, and the tests pin the mask bit through the live kernel rather than claiming to block time-namespace creation.
- That bit collision has a side effect the Python probe documents in place: a clone with CLONE_NEWTIME set reports exit signal 0x91, so the child is reaped with __WALL.
- The R side has no behavioral test for this flag. R cannot issue a clone() with chosen flags, and the R suite does not test the other namespace flags either. A C test hook or a Python helper in the R tests were both rejected: the first adds test-only code to the shipped library, and the second puts Python in the R suite.
- A shared tests/shared fixture for sandbox outcomes is deliberately left to kata dkev. roborev flagged the per-language duplication on each review; the dismissal reasoning is recorded on those jobs.

**Testing**

- pkg-py: ruff, pyrefly, and the full pytest suite pass (1869 passed). The BPF-interpreter clone test now parametrizes every namespace flag on all four architecture tables, and a new live test engages the filter in a child and asserts EPERM for a clone with the bit set. Verified on Linux arm64 in Docker: the live test passes, and fails when the flag is dropped from the mask.
- pkg-r: `sandbox.c` compiles without warnings on Linux, and the R CMD check CI jobs run the existing sandbox worker tests, which install this filter.

</details>

## Summary of R changes

@simonpcouch, FYI

[`sandbox.c`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/384/files#diff-321eed362d19f8c27f83b02082644b3d6065d9f177c6a6cfe80daa6fd2db69b0) adds CLONE_NEWTIME to the list of namespace flags its seccomp filter refuses in clone() calls, matching the Python filter; a run_r worker now gets EPERM permission error from `clone()` with the time-namespace bit set, which is the more technically correct behavior.

title: fix: screen abstract AF_UNIX sockets from the sandboxed worker
description:
On Linux, abstract Unix sockets have no actual filesystem path, so the sandbox's filesystem rules is not able to block them. As a result, agent-written code can reach local services on the host, such as D-Bus, even under `network = "none"`. This PR blocks that access in both packages. Under `network = "none"`, the seccomp filter now blocks the socket calls that take a peer address. On Linux 6.12 and later, Landlock also blocks these sockets under `network = "full"`.

> NB: Seccomp can't read the address of a network call the worker makes, so it only blocks these calls only under network = "none", where no network traffic is allowed anyway. Under network = "full", Landlock blocks abstract Unix sockets alone, but only on Linux 6.12 and later (which added the `LANDLOCK_SCOPE_ABSTRACT_UNIX_SOCKET` option).

<details>
<summary>Agent-written details</summary>

kata: hm25, and mv69 (the `socketcall` and `pidfd_getfd` blocks in R).

**Why these calls.** Abstract sockets have no filesystem path, so the Landlock path rules and the user-namespace sandbox cannot govern them. `socketpair()` stays open because it makes only AF_UNIX sockets. The filter blocks `sendto` only when the call has an address, because libc implements `send()` as `sendto()` with a NULL address. That form keeps socketpair traffic and the asyncio self-pipe working.

**Known gap.** On the user-namespace fallback tier with `network = "full"`, the host's abstract listeners stay reachable. The code and the vignette record this gap.

**Testing.** Ruff, pyrefly, pytest, testthat, and R CMD check pass. The R sandbox and worker tests also pass in a Linux 7.0 container (Landlock ABI 8), which runs the scoped Landlock ruleset. A Linux container showed the live behavior: `connect` and addressed `sendto` on a socketpair end return EPERM, and socketpair traffic and asyncio still work. A scoped worker gets EACCES from a host abstract listener, but it can reach a listener that it bound itself. [`tests/shared/sandbox-abstract-ipc.json`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/386/files#diff-9b515bf51d86fc61c6a8f3813347e465d5cbdc21994b6b2370487ea91acf4f63) pins the blocked calls and the Landlock ABI for both suites.

</details>

## Summary of R changes

@simonpcouch 

The worker's C sandbox in [`sandbox.c`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/386/files#diff-321eed362d19f8c27f83b02082644b3d6065d9f177c6a6cfe80daa6fd2db69b0) now blocks the same abstract-socket routes as the Python one. Model-written worker code can reach these sockets through a program it starts or a package with compiled code. 

Under `network = "none"`, `bind`, `connect`, `sendmsg`, `sendmmsg`, and `sendto` with an address now fail with EPERM, and `pidfd_getfd` fails in every network mode. A socketpair and a plain `send()` still work. 

On Linux 6.12 and later, a `network = "full"` worker also can no longer connect to an abstract socket that a host process bound. 

Tests added:

- [`test-sandbox-abstract-ipc.R`](https://github.com/posit-dev/commons/pull/386/files#diff-246d32f45150caf5c21cd16aea690383f9a91f5b0b7941f4db629fed0d5aaff6) checks the C source against the shared fixture.
